Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Courtauld Gallery, London, United Kingdom - Museum Tour

Stop 1: Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère

Address: The Courtauld Gallery, Somerset House, Strand, London WC2R 0RN, United Kingdom

Coordinates: 51.5117, -0.1162

Museum Information:

Orientation: You are about to explore The Courtauld Gallery in London. Your first stop is Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère. From three paces back, the oil surface of Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère comes alive with a peculiar shimmer—the glass bottles to the left, reflected in the mirror, refuse to align with their counterparts. Standing here, this visual riddle immediately unsettles the eye, setting the stage for the painting’s famous atmosphere of uncertainty.

The museum is open Monday to Sunday from 10:00 to 18:00. Admission is 11 pounds for adults; children 18 and under go free.

A Bar at the Folies-Bergère is Manet’s last major work, measuring 96 by 130 centimeters and executed in oil on canvas. The central figure, Suzon, was a barmaid who worked at the Folies-Bergère in the early 1880s and posed for Manet, lending the painting its immediate authenticity. The composition is disorienting: Suzon stands before a vast mirror that fractures space and perspective, while the misaligned bottles on the left side of the canvas are a deliberate choice by Manet, emphasizing the shifting realities and the crowded, electric atmosphere of the Folies-Bergère. The painting’s surface is layered with Manet’s rapid brushstrokes, creating a calculated disorder that makes visible the tensions of public performance and private self.

Despite his declining health, Manet exhibited the painting at the Paris Salon that year, though he held little hope of reaching his true audience. At this late moment in his career, he was confronting illness and the limits of his own body, yet he persisted in crafting a complex scene that encapsulated modern urban experience. The emotional force of the work emerges in the mirrored confusion and in Suzon’s ambiguous expression: poised amid spectacle, she appears both present and distant. Eventually, the painting made its way to London, joining the collection at The Courtauld Gallery, where it remains today.

Directions: Continue through The Courtauld Gallery — next is Courtauld Institute.

Stop 2: Courtauld Institute

Address: The Courtauld Institute of Art, Somerset House, Strand, London WC2R 0RN, United Kingdom

Coordinates: 51.5117, -0.1162

Orientation: Stand just before the marble balustrade, a few steps beyond the gallery’s central staircase. From here, the Courtauld Institute’s inscription comes into view above the archway—a reminder of the academic purpose that shapes every object in these halls. This vantage point ties the art you have already seen, such as Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, to the institution’s founding vision.

It originally operated out of Home House, an eighteenth-century townhouse designed by Robert Adam in Portman Square, before moving to Somerset House in 1989. Because of this foundation, the Courtauld Gallery, under the Samuel Courtauld Trust, began acquiring an exceptional collection of artworks. As a result, the Courtauld Institute quickly became the United Kingdom’s most prestigious institution for art history, housing one of the finest galleries in the country. The Courtauld Institute’s presence is not a painting or sculpture, but a living academic body woven through the museum’s walls. Its very founding required a turning point: Samuel Courtauld, a textile manufacturer whose fortune came from the industry’s looms, gave up private collecting to create a public institution. And Post-Impressionist paintings—acquired through years of thoughtful selection—were given, not held back, forming the backbone of the Gallery’s holdings. The consequence was profound: for the first time in Britain, students, scholars, and the general public could study original masterpieces under one roof, changing what could be learned and who could learn it. The marble, the oak-panelled seminar rooms, and even the way the light falls through the high windows reflect the Institute’s mission: research-led teaching, conservation, and the sharing of knowledge. The Institute offers world-renowned programs in the history, conservation, curation, and business of art. This is a place where art is not only displayed, but interrogated, restored, and understood anew with each generation. Our journey continues with a look at the innovative techniques of Georges Seurat.

Directions: Your final stop in The Courtauld Gallery: Georges Seurat.

Stop 3: Georges Seurat

Address: The Courtauld Gallery, Somerset House, Strand, London WC2R 0RN, United Kingdom

Coordinates: 51.5117, -0.1162

Orientation: As you stand here, take a half-step back from the Seurat wall and let your gaze settle just left of center—this is where the sequence of sea and port canvases thickens, and from this vantage, you can see not only the surface of each painting but the subtle shift in light and color from one to the next.

In the summer of 1890, Georges Seurat traveled to the coastal town of Gravelines in northern France. Working with small wooden panels and canvases, he completed four finished seascapes alongside painted oil studies, relying on systematic calculation and scientific theories to guide his placement of color. Just months after completing this coastal work, Seurat died suddenly in Paris in March 1891 at the age of thirty-one. The Courtauld has assembled seventeen of his twenty-four sea and port paintings, making this the largest such collection in the UK. In each work, Seurat applies his Neo-Impressionist method—tiny dots and dashes of paint laid side by side, a technique known as Pointillism. This method does not blend colors on the palette; instead, it lets the viewer’s own eye do the mixing, creating an optical vibration that mimics the shimmer of water and the haze of horizon. His eye for Seurat’s sea and port motifs was not just personal taste; it was a deliberate effort to anchor the collection with a body of work that represented a turning point in the evolution of modern art. This decision meant that The Courtauld would come to hold the largest group of Seurat’s marine subjects in Britain, giving scholars a unique opportunity to study the artist’s development up close. Another key figure, Georges Seurat himself, refused the established brushwork of his contemporaries. Instead, he pursued a methodical approach, applying dots of pure color to canvas in an effort to capture light as it truly behaves—fragmented, fleeting, never fixed. The consequence was not only a new visual language, but the creation of his monumental A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, a work that altered the direction of modern art and set the tone for what followed in European painting. Standing here, the physical properties of these works—oil on canvas, the near-mechanical repetition of marks—convey the cost of Seurat’s method: hours of labor, the risk of incomprehension, and the gamble that the public might not yet be ready for such analytic precision. The tension between precision and perception lingers in the air, a secret encoded in every dot.

This tour explores the interplay between public performance and private self, as seen in works like Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère and the innovative techniques of Seurat. This dynamic not only reflects the evolution of modern art but also invites us to reconsider how we perceive and engage with the world around us. That's 3 stops in all.
